title: Curriculum Vitae Fabio A
text:
Présentation
Maître de Conférences à l’ENSGSI, rattaché au laboratoire ERPI de l’Université de Lorraine. Ingénieur en mécanique formé à l’Université Nationale de Colombie, je suis titulaire d’un Master II en Management de l’Innovation et du Design Industriel, ainsi que d’un PhD en Génie des Systèmes Industriels de l’Université de Lorraine. Mon domaine de recherche se concentre sur la fabrication additive open source comme levier de développement industriel durable. Plus spécifiquement, j’étudie les nouvelles filières distribuées en circuit court pour la valorisation des matières plastiques recyclées via la fabrication additive. J’adopte une approche multi-échelle pour aborder les enjeux technologiques, filières associées et territoriaux, tout en privilégiant les collaborations avec divers acteurs. J’utilise différentes méthodologies pour améliorer, tester et expérimenter de nouveaux usages. Je possède une solide expérience dans la conduite de projets de recherche (EU, ANR) et de formation (ERASMUS+).

title: Introduction articule
text:
Plastic materials is a major paradox in the current era. The intrinsic plastic properties make them inexpensive, light-weight, and durable for a plethora of uses of in different applications, thus contributing to capitalistic societal development (Andrady and Neal 2009). Currently, 413 Mt in 2023 is produced worldwide (Dokl et al. 2024; Richie2023?), and about half of all plastics produced have been made in the last 15 years (Geyer et al. 2017). By 2050, the annual production is projected to increase between 902 Mt to 1124 Mt (OECD2022?). At the same time, their accumulation as macro-, micro-, and nanoplastics is generating harmful environmental and societal consequences for future generations (Porta 2021; De-la-Torre et al. 2021). Indeed, the widespread use and unethical disposal of plastics affects the ecosystems services in the terrestrial and aquatic compartiments (Kumar et al. 2021), which frames plastic pollution as a climate desition (Shen et al. 2020; Macreadie and Adyel 2025). Moreover, plastic pollution crisis is exacerbating pressures across multiple planetary boundaries (Biermann and Kim 2020; Villarrubia-Gómez et al. 2024), thereby threatening the safe operating space for humanity in which no global agreement is found up to date to limit to the virgin production (Villarrubia-Gómez et al. 2026; Vartanian 2025) In the case of France, roughly 4.5 million tonnes of plastic waste is generated per year, of which only 23% is recycled while 41% is incinerated and 36% is landfilled (MTE2025?). It is well below the 50% packaging-recycling target set by the European Union for 2025 (EEA2025_France?). Even with immediate and concerted action, around 79% of plastic waste is accumulated in the environment (Bundela and Pandey 2022; Hassan et al. 2024), and it is estimated that 710 Mt of plastic waste will enter aquatic and terrestrial ecosystems around 2040 (Lau et al. 2020).
Current centralized waste management systems remain structurally inadequate (Lerpiniere et al. 2025) to address the complex and systemic nature of plastic pollution (Salvia et al. 2021). Therefore, plastic waste management strategies within a circular economy framework (Tang 2025; Mallick et al. 2025) span a continuum from reuse and recycling approaches (including mechanical, chemical, and biological recycling) to thermolysis and energy recovery processes. Among these, mechanical recycling is widely recognized as the most environmentally favorable option (Klotz et al. 2023) for relatively clean and homogeneous streams of plastic and bioplastic waste, offering significantly lower environmental impacts compared to landfilling or incineration alternatives (Helbig et al. 2022). Therefore, recently efforts has increasingly turned attention to desing distributed approaches (Zhong and Pearce 2018; Cruz Sanchez et al. 2020) where sorting and recycling facilities close to the points where waste is generated (Gotti2025?; Chari2025?; CorreiadeMelo2024?) can be implemented.
Distributed approaches make possible to short collection distances and turn local plastic streams into marketable secondary materials (Simon 2019) creating opportunities for decentralized production (Prasad et al. 2024; Herrmann et al. 2020) for municipalities and small entrepreneurs (Spekkink et al. 2022). Indeed, a growing number of grassroots initiatives led by citizen networks, makerspaces, fablabs, and third places are experimenting with small-scale, community-based plastic recycling practices (Dijkstra and Planko 2023). Such practices can be understood as forms of urban manufacturing (Juraschek 2022; Croxford et al. 2020), promoting distributed production models as alternatives to globalized value chains (Priavolou et al. 2022; Cerdas et al. 2017). However, to make practical implementation of plastic circular economy depends on several operational (ie. routing problems (ref?) ), tactical (ie. infrasture design (ref?) ) and strategic (ie.) desicions from the sustainable supply chain perspective (Kumar et al. 2025) and enviromental performances (Kerdlap et al. 2021). Indeed, the distributed recycling approach frame the local territory as design space (Aviso2023?; Billal2025?) for a recovery network by pointing out design questions such as how many facilities to can be place in a local terrotory, what criteria can be use to place them considering the urban setups, and which areas they should serve as baseline. To answer thse questions is farm from trivial giving the structural barriers (Grafström 2025) (economic, institutional and regulatory, technological, and social) to consider in the supply and demand factors influencing the choice between virgin and recycled materials. Thereore, the major problem is that the design of distributed plastic recycling networks remains complex (ref?) because plastic waste is generated unevenly across a city (ref?) and trade-offs among diferent objectives (economic, environmental, operational) seldom favor the same layout (Cohen2025?). Reverse logistics, understood as the planning and control of the flows that recover discarded products for valorization or, failing that, safe disposal (Mallick2023?), provides that backbone (Govindan2015?). For instance, infrastructure is planned by treating economic, environmental, and social performance as joint objectives rather than cost alone (Eskandarpour2015?), spanning both strategic configuration and daily operation (Yu2020?; Joshi2022?), in which sorting and recycling centers are the nodes where recovery physically takes place (Shetty2022?). However, the major gap in the literature is that there is no methodological approach to include local spatial conditions, accessibility, and operational constraints (Mousania2026?; Zhang2023?) in the deisgn of distributed plastic recycling networks
Therefore, the main purpose of this paper is to propose a geographic information system (GIS) multi-objective optimization framework for the design of distributed plastic recycling collection networks. A case study of Nancy metropolitan area, France is presented to demonstrate its usefulness in order to identify whether a distributed configuration is viable to implement, in complement with traditional collection schemes (sulemana2018optimal?).
The remainder of the article is organized as follows. Section~\(\ref{sec:background}\) reviews the literature on distributed recycling and GIS-based waste-management planning and positions the contribution of this study. The problem is presented in Section~\(\ref{sec:problem}\) followed by the proposed two-stage framework in Section~\(\ref{sec:framework}\), and its mathematical formulation in Section~\(\ref{sec:model}\). Section~\(\ref{sec:Case_study}\) introduces the case study and its data, and Section~\(\ref{sec:results}\) reports the results together with a sensitivity analysis. The article then discusses policy and territorial implications and closes with the main conclusions.

title: Introduction articule
text:
1. Introduction
Plastic materials represent a major paradox of contemporary society. Their intrinsic properties, including low cost, lightweight structure, durability, and versatility, have enabled their widespread adoption across numerous industrial and consumer applications, contributing significantly to economic and societal development (Andrady and Neal 2009). Global plastic production reached approximately 413 million tonnes (Mt) in 2023 (Dokl et al. 2024; Richie2023?), with nearly half of all plastics ever manufactured having been produced within the preceding 15 years (Geyer et al. 2017). Annual production is projected to increase to between 902 and 1,124 Mt by 2050 (OECD2022?). However, the properties that make plastics valuable also contribute to their persistence in the environment, where they accumulate as macro-, micro-, and nanoplastics, posing substantial risks to ecosystems and human well-being (Porta 2021; De-la-Torre et al. 2021). The widespread consumption and inadequate disposal of plastic materials threaten ecosystem services across terrestrial and aquatic environments (Kumar et al. 2021), while plastic production and waste management contribute to climate change pressure (Shen et al. 2020; Macreadie and Adyel 2025). Furthermore, plastic pollution places increasing pressure on multiple planetary boundaries, threatening the safe operating space for humanity (Biermann and Kim 2020; Villarrubia-Gómez et al. 2024). Despite growing international recognition of these challenges, a binding global agreement to limit virgin plastic production has yet to be established (Villarrubia-Gómez et al. 2026; Vartanian 2025). In France, approximately 4.5 Mt of plastic waste is generated annually, of which only 23% is recycled, while 41% is incinerated and 36% is landfilled (MTE2025?). This recycling rate remains low in relation to the European Union’s 2025 target of 50% for plastic packaging waste, although the two indicators cover different waste streams (EEA2025_France?). At the global scale, approximately 79% of plastic waste generated historically has accumulated in landfills or the natural environment (Bundela and Pandey 2022; Hassan et al. 2024), and cumulative plastic leakage into terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems could reach 710 Mt by 2040 under a business-as-usual scenario (Lau et al. 2020). These trends underscore the need for more effective and territorially adapted plastic waste management strategies.
Existing centralized waste management systems face structural limitations in addressing the spatially dispersed and systemic nature of plastic pollution (Lerpiniere et al. 2025; Salvia et al. 2021). Within a circular economy framework, plastic waste management includes strategies ranging from reuse and material recycling (ie. mechanical, chemical, and biological), to thermolysis and energy recovery (Tang 2025; Mallick et al. 2025). Among these alternatives, mechanical recycling is generally considered an environmentally favorable option for relatively clean and homogeneous plastic waste streams (Klotz et al. 2023), offering lower environmental impacts than landfilling or incineration under suitable operating conditions (Helbig et al. 2022). In this context, increasing attention has been directed toward distributed recycling approaches (Zhong and Pearce 2018; Cruz Sanchez et al. 2020), in which collection, sorting, and recycling facilities are located closer to waste generation points (Gotti2025?; Chari2025?; CorreiadeMelo2024?).
Distributed recycling systems can reduce waste transportation distances and facilitate the transformation of locally generated plastic waste into marketable secondary materials (Simon 2019). By connecting local material recovery with decentralized manufacturing, these systems may create new opportunities for municipalities, small enterprises, and community-based initiatives to participate in circular value chains (Prasad et al. 2024; Herrmann et al. 2020; Spekkink et al. 2022). A growing number of grassroots initiatives, including citizen networks, makerspaces, fabrication laboratories (fablabs), and third places, are already experimenting with small-scale plastic recycling practices (Dijkstra and Planko 2023). These initiatives can be understood as emerging forms of urban manufacturing (Juraschek 2022; Croxford et al. 2020), promoting locally embedded production systems as alternatives or complements to conventional globalized value chains (Priavolou et al. 2022; Cerdas et al. 2017). Nevertheless, translating these initiatives into operationally viable circular economy systems requires coordinated decisions across strategic, tactical, and operational planning levels (Kumar et al. 2025). These include determining the configuration and location of recycling infrastructure, allocating waste generation areas to facilities, and organizing collection routes, while simultaneously accounting for environmental performance (Kerdlap et al. 2021).
From this perspective, distributed recycling shifts the focus of waste management toward the local territory as a spatial decision-making and network design problem (Aviso2023?; Billal2025?). The design of such networks raises several interrelated questions: How many collection and recycling facilities should be established within a given urban area? Where should these facilities be located, considering the existing urban structure and spatial accessibility? Which waste generation areas should each facility serve?. Addressing these questions is particularly challenging because the implementation of circular plastic systems is influenced by economic, institutional, regulatory, technological, and social barriers (Grafström 2025). Moreover, plastic waste generation is spatially heterogeneous, and alternative network configurations involve trade-offs among economic costs, environmental impacts, accessibility, and operational efficiency (Cohen2025?). Consequently, the design of distributed recycling networks requires an integrated approach capable of representing local spatial conditions while evaluating multiple, potentially conflicting objectives.
Reverse logistics provides a relevant conceptual and methodological foundation for addressing these challenges. It encompasses the planning, implementation, and control of material flows associated with the collection and recovery of discarded products for valorization or, when recovery is not feasible, safe disposal (Mallick2023?; Govindan2015?). Within sustainable supply chain management, reverse logistics network design increasingly incorporates economic, environmental, and social performance as interconnected objectives rather than focusing exclusively on cost minimization (Eskandarpour2015?). Such networks involve decisions across strategic and operational levels, including infrastructure configuration, facility location, service area allocation, and waste collection operations (Yu2020?; Joshi2022?). Collection, sorting, and recycling facilities constitute critical nodes within these networks, determining where material recovery activities take place and how waste flows are organized (Shetty2022?). However, despite advances in reverse logistics optimization, the integration of fine-scale territorial characteristics, spatial accessibility, and operational constraints into the multi-objective design of distributed plastic recycling networks remains insufficiently explored (Mousania2026?; Zhang2023?). This limitation is particularly relevant in urban contexts, where the spatial distribution of waste generation and the characteristics of the built environment can substantially influence the feasibility and performance of decentralized infrastructure.
To address this gap, this study proposes a geographic information system (GIS)-based multi-objective optimization framework for the spatial design of distributed plastic waste collection and recycling networks. The framework integrates territorial information and network design considerations to support decisions regarding facility location and the allocation of waste generation areas. Its applicability is demonstrated through a case study of the Nancy metropolitan area in France, where alternative distributed network configurations are evaluated to assess their potential feasibility and role as complements to conventional waste collection systems (sulemana2018optimal?). The study aims to provide a decision-support approach for planning territorially adapted plastic recovery infrastructure linking spatial analysis with multi-objective optimization.
The remainder of this article is organized as follows. Section~\(\ref{sec:background}\) reviews the literature on distributed recycling and GIS-based waste management planning and establishes the positioning of this study. Section~\(\ref{sec:problem}\) defines the network design problem, followed by the proposed two-stage framework in Section~\(\ref{sec:framework}\) and its mathematical formulation in Section~\(\ref{sec:model}\). Section~\(\ref{sec:Case_study}\) describes the Nancy metropolitan case study and the associated data, while Section~\(\ref{sec:results}\) presents the optimization results and sensitivity analysis. Finally, the article discusses the implications for territorial planning and circular economy policies before presenting the main conclusions.

title: Strengthening University tech transfer capabilities to support circular economy value chains for plastics in Latin America - TechTraPlastiCE
text:
Plastic materials have enhanced the current living standards of society, bringing a plethora of products at a cost and functional effectiveness level. However, under linear and “business-as-usual” thinking, the plastic waste is creating a worldwide societal issue leading to crossing the planetary boundaries of chemical pollution in our natural ecosystems given the longevity and the unknown long impacts (Villarrubia-Gómez et al. 2024).
In the past few decades, there has been a substantial increase in the yearly global plastic production, with it doubling between 2000 and 2019 to reach 460 million tones (Mt). The plastic market reached a value of 535 billion euros, and it also has an expected growth rate of 3.2%. Furthermore, it is expected to triple by 2060 according to the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) in its rapport of 2022. Of the nearly 10,000 million metric tons of virgin plastic material produced from 1950 to 2019, approximately 7,500 million metric tons have been converted into plastic waste. From 156 Mt in 2000 to 353 Mt in 2019, with nearly two-thirds originating from applications with lifespans of fewer than five years: packaging (40%), consumer products (12%), and textiles (11%) according to the European association Plastic Europe in their document of 2019. Out of this waste, only 55 Mt were collected for recycling, while 22 Mt became recycling residues requiring final disposal. In the end, 9% of the world’s plastic waste was recycled, 19% was incinerated, and almost 50% was deposited in sanitary landfills. The remaining 22% was either disposed of in uncontrolled dumpsites, burned in open pits, or leaked into the environment.



Today, a systemic transition towards a just and safe circular economy needs to be made in the plastic value chain, understanding the technical, organizational, social, and legislative leverage points. Then, alternatives to mitigate the environmental impact need to be co-created in a trans-disciplinary approach in the global south as in the European countries.
Therefore, the Higher Educational Institutions (HEI) have a major role to play in this worldwide societal issue. In the context of the green transition, universities have much to offer in joint green innovation projects with business, government and citizens. As hubs of diverse expertise, universities are uniquely placed to build interdisciplinary teams and bridge gaps between society and industry. Their regional ties also enable them to engage with the local ecosystem. Certainly, this is enframed as the HEI’s third mission to play a major role in the exchange of knowledge, know-how and technology among socio-economical stakeholders with the purpose to stimulate a transition including the whole stakeholders in the plastic value chain from pick-up waste collectors, consumers and industry ecosystems. As there is no unique model to deal with plastic waste, proposed solutions should take into account the local ecosystem of stakeholders and be co-created in each country.

Today, a systemic transition towards a just and safe circular economy needs to be made in the plastic value chain, understanding the technical, organizational, social, and legislative leverage points. Then, alternatives to mitigate the environmental impact need to be co-created in a trans-disciplinary approach in the global south as in the European countries.
Therefore, the Higher Educational Institutions (HEI) have a major role to play in this worldwide societal issue. In the context of the green transition, universities have much to offer in joint green innovation projects with business, government and citizens. As hubs of diverse expertise, universities are uniquely placed to build interdisciplinary teams and bridge gaps between society and industry. Their regional ties also enable them to engage with the local ecosystem. Certainly, this is enframed as the HEI’s third mission to play a major role in the exchange of knowledge, know-how and technology among socio-economical stakeholders with the purpose to stimulate a transition including the whole stakeholders in the plastic value chain from pick-up waste collectors, consumers and industry ecosystems. As there is no unique model to deal with plastic waste, proposed solutions should take into account the local ecosystem of stakeholders and be co-created in each country.

text:
Their potential toxicity is not simply chemically mediated as for most pollutants but driven by very complex, numerous and diverse phenomena (fragmentation, diffusion, interaction and so on) occurring during their extremely long, diverse and obscure lifespans, resulting
The success of plastics as a material has been substantial; they have proved versatile for use in a range of types and forms, including natural polymers, modified natural polymers, thermosetting plastics, thermoplastics and, more recently, biodegradable plastics.
Plastics have a range of unique properties. They can be used at a very wide range of temperatures, are chemical- and light-resistant and they are very strong and tough, but can be easily worked as a hot melt. They opens up the technical properties in order to sophistication of the product design.
Human society arrived to the plastic age (Thompson2009a?). Although plastic materials have contributed substantially to societal development, they have increasingly become a paradox for human progress. Humans have benefited from the use of polymers since approximately 1600 BC, when the ancient Mesoamericans first processed natural rubber into balls, figurines and bands. Nevertheless, it was not until the \(19^{th}\) that the development of modern synthetic thermoplastics began. In 1839, Goodyear developed vulcanized rubber, and Eduard Simon, a German apothecary, discovered polystyrene (PS). The Bakelite was the first truly synthetic polymer developed by Belgian chemist Leo Baekeland in 1907. Since then, experimental work have continued on natural/synthetic polymers givin main inventions between the two World Wars: cellophane in 1913, then polyvinyl chloride (PVC) in 1927, nylon in 1938, and polyethylene in 1942 (Andrady2009?; Chalmin 2019). The development of synthetic polymers are typically prepared by polymerization of monomers derived from oil or gas. These synthetic polymers include several chemical additives to help in the color, processability, thermal/mechanical properties. It was not until the 1940s and 1950s, that mass production of everyday plastic items really started to take place (Thompson2009a?) and many other plastics were subsequently developed over the next few decades.
However, plastics production and consumption is cause growing — and in some ways existential — risks for people and ecosystems. Currently, 413 Mt in 2023 is produced worldwide (plasticseurope2024?) and about half of all plastics produced have been made in the last 15 years. By 2050, the annual production is projected to increase by 2–3 times arriving to a global plastic production between 902 Mt to 1124 Mt. It is proved that less than 10% of this production actually have been recycled since 1950 (Geyer2017?). The compounding effect of plastic waste accumulation in the different ecosystems is an imminent risk for all biotic ecosystems. Currently, 79% of this widely anthropogenic chemical subtance is accumulated in the environment, having a ubiquitous presence and polluting almost all compartiments of the ecosystem (Bundela and Pandey 2022; Hassan et al. 2024). Indeed, accumulation stock of plastic particles (macro, micro, nano) in the environment is starting to be used as stratigraphic markers in field archaeological practice as indicators of modern or recently disturbed deposits (Zalasiewicz et al. 2016). This proves that it is a wicked problem, and one of the main markers of human presence on Earth.
The major contradiction of plastic materials is that, while the first steps related to the production, usage and short-term post-usage (incineration, recycling) are relatively well known, the long-term that occurs after discarding (after reuse and recycling) remain largely unclear in its life cycle. After discarding, conventional petrochemical plastics have been discovered behaving differently relative to traditional materials (i.e. metal, wood, glass). Plastic wastes do not solubilize slowly like dense materials, such as glass or metals, to reintegrate into silica or iron cycles and mineralize soils and water. They are also not digested by the micro-organisms naturally present in soils like natural organic materials, such as paper, cotton and leather, to reintegrate in the natural carbon cycle. In other words, they do not reintegrate into one of the relatively well-known biogeochemical cycles of the elements of our ecosystems (Gontard et al. 2022). Therefore, this chemical polution is included as one of the planetary boundaries(O’Neill et al. 2018; Biermann and Kim 2020), which affects humanity for reminding within the safe operating limits.
In 2022, United Nations Environment Assembly (UNEA) of the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) proposed a draft resolution in order to adopt an international legally binding instrument by the year 2024 (Bundela and Pandey 2022). The draft resolution shed ligths on two overarching themes: 1) responsible consumption and prodution (SDG-12), and 2) circular economy principles. UNEA’s draft resolution was aimed “To promote sustainable production and consumption of plastics through, among other things, product design and environmentally sound waste management, including through resource efficiency and circular economy approaches” (UNEP 2022). In principle, 175 member stated on the UN agreed to this proposition (Arora et al. 2024). One of the major advances was to the recognition of the seriousness of micro/nano-plastics (in marine and soil compartiments, and in the human health), which is a transboundary environmental issue (Landrigan et al. 2025). However, after five sessions of the Intergovernmental Negotiation Committee (INC) so far (last at Geneva in August 2025), an agreement that all parties can abide by has remained elusive. Two main harsh truths were exposed. First, even if no state formally objects this agreement, a consensus on the treaty text cannot be reached. And second, securing a high-ambition treaty is going to require launching a new process outside the United Nations (UN) framework.
Entering in a more deep analysis of this controverse, it is possible deligthted three main aspect: 1) defition of the plastic problem, 2) procedural deadlock and 3) delays in the ambition of the scope of the treaty (March and Winton 2025).
Concerning the definition issues, some countries have proposed narrow definition of ‘plastic pollution’, limiting the definition to plastic products that have been mismanaged at the of life (March and Winton 2025). Indeed, for certain nations, it was about improving waste management, recycling systems and circular economies. While for others, it meant curbing the manufacture of primary polymers. Discrepancies also appeared in importance of the plastic value chain of the nations (Ivanova 2025). Plastics manufacturing implies economic and political stability for some nations. Whereas for small island states and vulnerable coastal areas, plastic pollution threatens human survival. The negotiations contrasted the economic realities of some countries with the ecological urgencies tha imply this status-quo in some nations. This diversity of perspectives in defining the nature of the problem leads to an ambiguity that is part of a geopolitical division. Another definition issues was the full extent of the ‘lifecycle of plastics’, where some nations argued a position that lifecyclee begins only after a plastic product has been manufactured. Fortunalety, a more systemic definition was adopted as: “all the activities and outcomes associated with the production and consumption of plastic materials, products and services — from raw material extraction and processing (refining, cracking, polymerization) to design, manufacturing, packaging, distribution, use (and reuse), maintenance and end-of-life management, including segregation, collection, sorting, recycling and disposal”. The implication was that without an appropriated definition of the full lifecycle, the treaty risk to becomeing a waste-management agreement rather than a systemic answer tot the plastic pollution (Simon et al. 2021)
On the other hand, another element to consider relies on the lack of a clear desicion making process either through voting or consensus. Consequently, a single dissenting country is at present empowered to veto important decisions. This allows a small number of countries to block progress, leading, for example, to the blocking of any intersessional work after INC-3 (Nairobi, 2023) and to a substantial reduction in the mandate of the intersessional work agreed at INC-4 (Ottawa, 2024). When a process works on consensus and you have a few countries refusing to move on certain things, it becomes very difficult to make progress. Indeed, a number of countries — and UNEP itself — are strongly opposed to the introduction of voting, so that would be challenging to implement.”
Finnaly, the ambition scope remains is major element of controverse. A High Ambition Coalition 1 of countries, more than 100 UN member states, have supported setting global targets for reducing the production of primary plastic polymers to sustainable levels. In fact, recent research suggests that capping primary plastic production at 2020 levels could significantly curb plastic pollution (Pottinger et al. 2024). Addressing upstream plastic production is essential to ending plastic pollution However, the main issue is that a handful of primarily oil-producing countries whose economies are structured around fossil fuels, bolstered by corporations with similar vested interests, opposes production caps and prefers to focus on downstream waste management and recycling instead.

title: Multi-material distributed recycling via material extrusion: recycled high density polyethylene and poly (ethylene terephthalate) mixture
text: The high volume of plastic waste and the extremely low recycling rate have created a serious challenge worldwide. Local distributed recycling and additive manufacturing (DRAM) offers a solution by economically incentivizing local recycling. One DRAM technology capable of processing large quantities of plastic waste is fused granular fabrication, where solid shredded plastic waste can be reused directly as 3D printing feedstock. This study presents an experimental assessment of multimaterial recycling printability using two of the most common thermoplastics in the beverage industry, polyethylene terephthalate (PET) and high-density polyethylene (HDPE), and the feasibility of mixing PET and HDPE to be used as a feedstock material for large-scale 3-D printing. After the material collection, shredding, and cleaning, the characterization and optimization of parameters for 3D printing were performed. Results showed the feasibility of printing a large object from rPET/ rHDPE flakes, reducing production costs by up to 88%.

text:
, Libro III - Paragrafro 6

Escribir. Algo tan básico pero al mismo tiempo tan complejo. Escribir lo que uno piensa puede ser una distracción, un catalizador, o incluso, un medio de relajación para ciertas personas. No importa el propósito, creo que lo importante es poder transcribir en letras las cosas por las que nuestra mente divaga constantemente.
No tengo un punto importante a desarrollar en esta entrada de blog. Solo quiero decir que escribir, parece como una actividad que vagamente hacemos por nosotros mismos. O en todo caso ese es mi caso. Si no tengo un articulo, proyecto, o algo externo por el cual deba escribir. Probablemente no escribo. Sin embargo, quiero comprobar si el hecho de poner en letras alguna parte de nuestra consciencia; puede ser en cierto modo sea un llamado al destino para que las letras que uno pone en un papel (o sitio web) algún día se conviertan en realidad. ¿Será una especie de pócima mágica para que la vida que uno quiere aparezca? ¿Se hace realidad lo que uno escribe? ¿Es que Dios juega a los dados cuando uno no escribe lo que piensa para su vida?
No sé, muy difícilmente lo sabré. Solo puedo decir que escribir es la primera palabra que se me viene a la mente y a partir escribo para no olvidar. Escribo para clarificar el ser. Escribo para expresar con palabras las ilusiones del alma. Escribir es como armarse con una espada y un escudo para atravesar el bosque oscuro y peligroso de nuestro inconsciente, y realizar un viaje del héroe, como lo describiría Joseph campbell

title: Meditaciones: Lo importante es comenzar
text:
Ten presente, pues, estas prescripciones y deja a un lado todo lo demás. No olvides tampoco que la vida se limita para cada uno de nosotros al tiempo presente, que sólo es un fugaz intervalo; el resto de la existencia no existe, o es incierto. Por consiguiente, la vida de todo ser no representa casi nada; el lugar donde transcurre no es más que un rincón insignificante de la Tierra, y la reputación más duradera que uno deja tras de sí apenas si vale algo, pues se transmite mediante una sucesión a individuos insignificantes que, a su vez deben morir también, que no se conocen a ellos mismos y que, como es natural, conocen mucho menos todavía al que murió hace mucho tiempo.

Meditaciones, Libro III - Paragrafro 6

Los grandes cambios en la vida comienzan con acciones concretas. Acciones de hecho pequeñas. Muy pequeñas, que casi son imperceptibles para nuestra conciencia tan agitada en un mundo que no tiene cabida para la reflexión en silencio. Y aun así, estos cambios en silencio representan los gigantescos terremotos que hacen evolucionar las trayectorias de vida.
Para mí, este punto de inflexión se resume en escribir. Cerrar los ojos, mirarme al interior y poder deslizar mis dedos en un teclado donde intento no poner freno alguno a lo que estoy poniendo en la realidad. Se resume en sacar de la cabeza todas las lanas enredaderas que pueden hacer dentro de un cerebro que lidia por encontrar un propósito en la vida. Porque la vida es corta. Está hecha de esos segundos que llamamos el presente. Y que si no somos conscientes, se pasan sin ser admirados en su justo valor.
Escribir es aclarar y escuchar en los pensamientos. Y al momento de escribir esto, mis ojos lloran de poder exprimir lo que siento en esta época de mi vida de Octubre 2024. Un periodo donde cambios pequeños pueden tener una incidencia gigante en mi existencia y paso por esta tierra.
Este escrito no tiene más propósito que poder comenzar con algo. Empezar con cosas insignificantes. El acto de empezar es como la semilla que se pone en un jardín. Nunca seremos totalmente en control del resultado. Sin embargo, en honor al estoicismo, quiero hacer la acción que hace parte de mi control. Tiene el propósito de poder sacar afuera, valga la redundancia, las cosas que se llevan dentro. Tiene como objetivo aclarar un camino hacia donde apuntar. Ya que, durante el trayecto que tiene mi existencia he perdido el rumbo.
Lo llamo meditaciones en honor al Estoicismo, que aunque es una filosofía que resuena en mi, siento qué es mas un camino de vida a seguir.

title: Enhancing vibration damping properties of additively manufactured viscoelastic structures through process parameter optimization
text: With the increasing use of additive manufacturing (AM) in diverse fields, printed structures are inevitably exposed to vibrations, which can result in fracture, fatigue, and noise. Present study aims to enhance the damping characteristics of the final part by incorporating viscoelastic materials into the primary structure using multi-material AM. The effects of process parameters on the vibration damping characteristics of printed viscoelastic structures were investigated through modal analysis and design of experiments. Results show that higher nozzle temperature, smaller layer height, lower deposition speed and smaller raster angle contribute to higher resonant frequencies and loss factors of the final parts.

title: Global Plastics Treaty: Controversy or Collapse?
text:
Human society arrived to the plastic age (Thompson et al. 2009). Although plastic materials have contributed substantially to societal development, they have increasingly become a paradox for human progress. Humans have benefited from the use of polymers since approximately 1600 BC, when the ancient Mesoamericans first processed natural rubber into balls, figurines and bands. Nevertheless, it was not until the \(19^{th}\) that the development of modern synthetic thermoplastics began. In 1839, Goodyear developed vulcanized rubber, and Eduard Simon, a German apothecary, discovered polystyrene (PS). The Bakelite was the first truly synthetic polymer developed by Belgian chemist Leo Baekeland in 1907. Since then, experimental work have continued on natural/synthetic polymers giving main inventions between the two World Wars: cellophane in 1913, then polyvinyl chloride (PVC) in 1927, nylon in 1938, and polyethylene in 1942 (Andrady and Neal 2009; Chalmin 2019). The development of synthetic polymers are typically prepared by polymerization of monomers derived from oil or gas. These synthetic polymers include several chemical additives to help in color, processability, and thermal/mechanical properties. It was not until the 1940s and 1950s, that mass production of everyday plastic items really started to take place (Thompson et al. 2009) and many other plastics were subsequently developed over the next few decades.
However, plastics production and consumption is cause growing — and in some ways existential — risks for people and ecosystems. Currently, 413 Mt in 2023 is produced worldwide as illustrated by Figure 1, and about half of all plastics produced have been made in the last 15 years. By 2050, the annual production is projected to increase by 2–3 times arriving to a global plastic production between 902 Mt to 1124 Mt. It is proved that less than 10% of this production actually have been recycled since 1950 (Geyer et al. 2017). The compounding effect of plastic waste accumulation in the different ecosystems is an imminent risk for all biotic ecosystems. Currently, 79% of this widely anthropogenic chemical subtance is accumulated in the environment, having a ubiquitous presence and polluting almost all compartiments of the ecosystem (Bundela and Pandey 2022; Hassan et al. 2024). Landrigan et al. (2025) developed a diagram summarising plastics’ impacts on health as presented in Figure 2. Most of these established harms are mediated by exposure to plastic chemicals while others might be due to micro/nano plastic (MNP) particles. Indeed, accumulation stock of MNP in the environment is starting to be used as stratigraphic markers in field archaeological practice as indicators of modern or recently disturbed deposits (Zalasiewicz et al. 2016). This proves that it is a wicked problem, and one of the main markers of human presence on Earth.
The major contradiction of plastic materials is that, while the first steps related to the production, usage and short-term post-usage (incineration, recycling) are relatively well known, the long-term that occurs after discarding (after reuse and recycling) remain largely unclear in its life cycle. After discarding, conventional petrochemical plastics have been discovered behaving differently relative to traditional materials (i.e. metal, wood, glass). Plastic wastes do not solubilize slowly like dense materials, such as glass or metals, to reintegrate into silica or iron cycles and mineralize soils and water. They are also not digested by the micro-organisms naturally present in soils like natural organic materials, such as paper, cotton and leather, to reintegrate in the natural carbon cycle. In other words, they do not reintegrate into one of the relatively well-known biogeochemical cycles of the elements of our ecosystems (Gontard et al. 2022). Therefore, this chemical polution is included as one of the planetary boundaries(O’Neill et al. 2018; Biermann and Kim 2020), which affects humanity for reminding within the safe operating limits.
In 2022, United Nations Environment Assembly (UNEA) of the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) proposed a draft resolution in order to adopt an international legally binding instrument by the year 2024 (Bundela and Pandey 2022). The draft resolution shed ligths on two overarching themes: 1) responsible consumption and prodution (SDG-12), and 2) circular economy principles. UNEA’s draft resolution was aimed “To promote sustainable production and consumption of plastics through, among other things, product design and environmentally sound waste management, including through resource efficiency and circular economy approaches” (UNEP 2022). In principle, 175 member stated on the UN agreed to this proposition (Arora et al. 2024). One of the major advances was to the recognition of the seriousness of micro/nano-plastics (in marine and soil compartiments, and in the human health), which is a transboundary environmental issue (Landrigan et al. 2025). The draft resolution made possible the establishment of an Intergovernmental Negotiating Committee (INC) with an ambitious objective of concluding an international legally binding instrument by the end of 2024. Five sessions were made since 20221.
Guo and Hu (2025) summarised the key negotiation milestones and issues of the treaty from 2022 to 2025. However, after five sessions of the INC so far (last at Geneva in August 2025), an agreement that all parties can abide by has remained elusive. Two main harsh truths were exposed. First, even if no state formally objects this agreement, a consensus on the treaty text cannot be reached. And second, securing a high-ambition treaty may require launching a new process outside the United Nations (UN) framework.
Entering in a more deep analysis of this controversy, it is possible elucidate three main aspects: 1) definition of the plastic problem, 2) procedural deadlock and 3) delays in the ambition of the scope of the treaty.
Concerning the definition issues, some countries have proposed narrow definition of ‘plastic pollution’, limiting the definition to plastic products that have been mismanaged at the of life (March and Winton 2025). Indeed, for certain nations, it was about improving waste management, recycling systems and circular economies. While for others, it meant curbing the manufacture of primary polymers. Discrepancies also appeared in importance of the plastic value chain (Ivanova 2025). Plastic industry implies economic and political stability for some nations. Whereas for small island states and vulnerable coastal areas, plastic pollution threatens human survival. The negotiations contrasted the economic realities of some countries with the ecological urgencies that imply plastic status-quo in some nations. This diversity of perspectives in defining the nature of the problem leads to an ambiguity that is part of a geopolitical division. Likewise, the definition of the ‘full extent of the lifecycle of plastics’ was a controversy. Some nations argued a position that lifecycle begins only after a plastic product has been manufactured. While for other nations, lifecycle begins from the extraction stage.
Fortunaletly, a systemic definition of the lifecycle of plastic was adopted as: “all the activities and outcomes associated with the production and consumption of plastic materials, products and services — from raw material extraction and processing (refining, cracking, polymerization) to design, manufacturing, packaging, distribution, use (and reuse), maintenance and end-of-life management, including segregation, collection, sorting, recycling and disposal”. The implication was that, without an appropriated definition of the full lifecycle, the treaty risk to becoming a waste-management agreement rather than a systemic answer of the plastic pollution (Simon et al. 2021)
The second element of controversy to consider relies on the lack of a clear desicion-making process, either through voting or consensus. A single dissenting country is at present empowered to veto important decisions. Consequently, this allows a small number of countries to block progress, leading for example, to the blocking of any intersessional work after INC-3 (Nairobi, 2023) and to a substantial reduction in the mandate of the intersessional work agreed at INC-4 (Ottawa, 2024). When a process works on consensus and you have a few countries refusing to move on certain things, it becomes very difficult to make progress. Indeed, a number of countries — and UNEP itself — are strongly opposed to the introduction of voting, so that would be challenging to implement.
Finally, the ambition scope remains is major element of controverse. According to Ivanova (2025), the negotiations have stalled partly because a false morality of ambition versus obstruction that took hold. This kind of narrative between ‘heroes versus villains’ has obscured the complex realities at stake. From one hand, there is the High Ambition Coalition of countries2 that have supported a treaty with global targets for reducing the production of primary plastic polymers to sustainable levels, elimination of single-use plastics, bans on hazardous additives, and regulate the entire life cycle of plastic. On the other hand, a smaller group, the so-called Like-Minded Group 3, that aims for a voluntary Global Plastics Treaty, opposing upstream measures and prioritising only waste management. Nonetheles to say that recent research suggests that capping primary plastic production at 2020 levels could significantly curb plastic pollution (Pottinger et al. 2024). Addressing upstream plastic production is essential to ending plastic pollution (Spring et al. 2025). There is a third group of countries whose position has been more difficult to understand, including Brazil and China.
While plastics treaty ended without an official agreement, it did not collapse. A third part of the Fifth Session (INC-5.3) will take place on 7 February 2026, Geneva, Switzerland. I consider that despite the divergents perspectives, there are elements that all parties converge around, namely: leviers of sustainable product design, resource efficiency, waste management and circular economy principles (Ivanova 2025). Identifying areas of convergence and of contention is key. Indeed, Guo and Hu (2025) pointed out that an effective treaty on plastics pollution control requires major players such as China, India and the United States to be a part of. Moreover, one structural element to hightlight is that there is no formal system for sharing reliable scientific information on plastics within the negotiations. Scientists can attend the talks, either as observers or as part of official delegations, but their research does not directly feed into the documents guiding the discussions. Recently , the establishment of the Intergovernmental Science-Policy Panel on Chemicals, Waste and Pollution seeks to narrow the gap. One of the panel’s first tasks should be to bring clarity to the debate by building a shared understanding of the evidence on the issues at stake. The first meeting will be in Geneva next February. This is a controverse that will continue its journey in the following years to come.

title: Logique, Histoire & philosophie de la logique
text:
En français

Pierre Wagner, Logique et philosophie. Manuel d’introduction pour les étudiants du supérieur, Ellipses, 2014, 360 p. Niveau : initiation

Pierre Wagner enseigne la logique aux étudiants de philosophie de l’université Paris 1 Panthéon-Sorbonne, et ce manuel est directement pensé pour ce public. Il expose les concepts et les méthodes de base de la logique formelle (calcul des propositions, calcul des prédicats) sans supposer de formation mathématique, tout en montrant ce que ces outils apportent à des questions proprement philosophiques. C’est sans doute le compagnon le plus naturel de ce cours.

Gilles Dowek, Les démonstrations et les algorithmes. Introduction à la logique et à la calculabilité, Éditions de l’École polytechnique, 2010, 194 p. Niveau : intermédiaire à avancé

Issu de l’enseignement de Gilles Dowek à l’École polytechnique, ce livre introduit les notions de démonstration, de fonction calculable, de modèle et d’ensemble. Il conduit jusqu’au théorème d’indécidabilité de Church (dont le théorème d’incomplétude de Gödel apparaît comme un corollaire), puis aborde la recherche automatique de démonstrations et les démonstrations constructives. Idéal pour qui s’intéresse aux liens entre logique et informatique.
L’introduction et la table des matières sont en ligne sur la page de l’auteur : introduction (PDF), table des matières (PDF). Traduction anglaise : Proofs and Algorithms. An Introduction to Logic and Computability, Springer, coll. « Undergraduate Topics in Computer Science », 2011.

René Cori et Daniel Lascar, Logique mathématique. Cours et exercices corrigés, 2 tomes, préface de Jean-Louis Krivine, Dunod, coll. « Sciences Sup », 2003 (1re éd. Masson, 1993)


Tome 1 : Calcul propositionnel, algèbres de Boole, calcul des prédicats
Tome 2 : Fonctions récursives, théorème de Gödel, théorie des ensembles, théorie des modèles Niveau : avancé

La référence française classique en logique mathématique, issue de l’équipe de logique de l’université Paris 7. Le premier tome couvre le calcul propositionnel, les algèbres de Boole, le calcul des prédicats et les théorèmes de complétude ; le second traite de la récursivité, des théorèmes de Gödel, de la théorie des ensembles et de la théorie des modèles. Très rigoureux, chaque chapitre est accompagné de nombreux exercices corrigés : c’est l’ouvrage à ouvrir si vous voulez faire de la logique « en mathématicien ».
Traduction anglaise : Mathematical Logic. A Course with Exercises, 2 vol., trad. Donald H. Pelletier, Oxford University Press, 2000–2001. 4. Robert Blanché et Jacques Dubucs, La logique et son histoire, Armand Colin, coll. « U », 1996 Niveau : initiation à intermédiaire (lecture d’accompagnement)
Il s’agit de l’édition revue du classique de Robert Blanché, La logique et son histoire d’Aristote à Russell (1970), dont Jacques Dubucs a complété la partie finale pour couvrir le XXe siècle. Plutôt qu’un manuel d’exercices, c’est une mise en perspective : on y suit la logique d’Aristote aux Stoïciens, aux médiévaux, à Leibniz, puis à la logique mathématique moderne.
En anglais 5. Volker Halbach, The Logic Manual, Oxford University Press, 2010 Niveau : initiation
C’est le manuel du cours d’introduction à la logique suivi par les étudiants en philosophie d’Oxford. Court (environ 200 pages) et très clair, il couvre la logique propositionnelle et la logique des prédicats avec identité, leur sémantique (avec des définitions précises de la vérité et de la satisfaction) et la déduction naturelle. Un site compagnon propose des exercices, des exemples et des sujets d’examen.

Graham Priest, Logic: A Very Short Introduction, 2e éd., Oxford University Press, coll. « Very Short Introductions », 2017 (1re éd. 2000) Niveau : initiation (lecture de découverte)

Un petit livre de poche, vivant et sans technicité, où chaque chapitre part d’une question philosophique : l’existence de Dieu, la réalité du temps, le vague, les conditionnels, l’identité à travers le changement… Priest y présente aussi bien la logique classique que des logiques non classiques, et la deuxième édition ajoute des développements sur les algorithmes, les axiomes et la démonstration en mathématiques.

Nicholas J. J. Smith, Logic: The Laws of Truth, Princeton University Press, 2012 Niveau : initiation à intermédiaire

Un manuel volumineux (plus de 500 pages) et remarquablement clair, consacré à la logique classique du premier ordre avec identité. Sa particularité est de concevoir la logique comme l’étude des « lois de la vérité » plutôt que du raisonnement, et d’expliquer non seulement comment fonctionnent les outils formels, mais aussi pourquoi ils sont construits ainsi. Les tables de vérité et la méthode des arbres y occupent une place centrale. Très bon choix pour qui veut un manuel complet pour travailler seul.

Theodore Sider, Logic for Philosophy, Oxford University Press, 2010 Niveau : intermédiaire à avancé

Conçu pour des étudiants avancés de licence et des débutants en master de philosophie, ce livre vise à donner la logique nécessaire pour lire la philosophie contemporaine. Il privilégie l’étendue à la profondeur : après la logique propositionnelle et la logique des prédicats (et leurs variantes non standard), il traite de la logique modale propositionnelle et quantifiée, des contrefactuels et de la logique modale bidimensionnelle. Il ne démontre pas les grands résultats métalogiques (complétude, indécidabilité), mais reste très accessible sans formation mathématique poussée.

John MacFarlane, Philosophical Logic: A Contemporary Introduction, Routledge, coll. « Routledge Contemporary Introductions to Philosophy », 2021 Niveau : intermédiaire (PDF en libre accès)

Un excellent « deuxième livre », pensé pour des étudiants ayant déjà suivi un cours d’introduction. MacFarlane y examine les limites, les présupposés et les alternatives de la logique classique du premier ordre : quantificateurs généralisés, logiques modales et déontiques, conditionnels, conséquence logique (par les modèles ou par les preuves), remise en cause de principes comme le modus ponens ou l’élimination de la double négation, explosion et contradictions, rapport entre logique et raisonnement, vague. Chaque chapitre s’organise autour de lectures conseillées et propose des exercices.
Avec l’accord de l’éditeur, l’auteur met à disposition un PDF du livre (version révisée) sur sa page, où l’on trouve aussi les errata. 10. Dirk van Dalen, Logic and Structure, Springer, coll. « Universitext », 5e éd., 2013 (1re éd. 1980) Niveau : avancé
Un manuel de logique mathématique de référence, l’un des premiers à avoir systématiquement utilisé la déduction naturelle de Gentzen. Il couvre la logique propositionnelle et des prédicats, le théorème de complétude et ses applications, la logique du second ordre, la logique intuitionniste, la normalisation des démonstrations et le théorème de Gödel.
Version électronique sur SpringerLink Manuels en ligne, en libre accès Ces deux manuels complets sont gratuits et téléchargeables légalement. Ils sont en anglais.

P. D. Magnus et Tim Button, revu et augmenté par Aaron Thomas-Bolduc et Richard Zach, forall x: Calgary. An Introduction to Formal Logic, Open Logic Project Niveau : initiation (licence CC BY 4.0)

Un manuel complet, très proche du contenu de ce cours : validité des arguments, logique des fonctions de vérité et tables de vérité, logique du premier ordre avec identité, formalisation d’énoncés de la langue naturelle, déduction naturelle « à la Fitch ». Il aborde aussi quelques sujets plus avancés (logique modale, adéquation, complétude fonctionnelle) et propose des exercices corrigés.
Page du livre PDF du livre · PDF des corrigés · version accessible (dyslexie) Version HTML à lire en ligne 12. Johan van Benthem, Hans van Ditmarsch, Jan van Eijck et Jan Jaspars, Logic in Action, nouvelle édition, 2016 Niveau : initiation à intermédiaire
Issu d’un projet de cours ouvert de l’Institute for Logic, Language and Computation d’Amsterdam, ce manuel a été utilisé notamment à Amsterdam, Pékin et Stanford. Il présente d’abord les systèmes classiques (logique propositionnelle, syllogistique d’Aristote, logique des prédicats), puis ce qui fait son originalité : la logique de la connaissance et de l’information (logique épistémique), la logique de l’action (logique dynamique) et les liens entre logique et théorie des jeux. Une dernière partie revient sur les méthodes : tableaux sémantiques, déduction naturelle, et usage de la logique en programmation (Prolog). Idéal pour découvrir la logique comme discipline carrefour entre philosophie, mathématiques, informatique et sciences cognitives.

Presentación
Profesor en la École Nationale Supérieure en Génie des Systèmes et de l’Innovation –ENSGSI-, adscrita al laboratorio de investigación Équipe de Recherche sur les Processus Innovatifs – ERPI- de la Université de Lorraine en Francia. Ingeniero mecánico formado en la Universidad Nacional de Colombia, poseo un Máster II en Gestión de la Innovación y Diseño Industrial, así como un doctorado en Ingeniería de Sistemas Industriales por la Université de Lorraine. Mi área de investigación se centra en la fabricación aditiva de código abierto como palanca para el desarrollo industrial sostenible. Más concretamente, estoy estudiando nuevos canales de distribución cortos para la recuperación de plásticos reciclados mediante la fabricación aditiva. Adopto un enfoque multiescala para abordar las cuestiones tecnológicas, industriales y territoriales asociadas, al tiempo que favorezco la colaboración con diversas partes interesadas. Utilizo distintas metodologías para mejorar, probar y experimentar nuevos usos. Tengo una sólida experiencia en la dirección de proyectos de investigación (EU H2020, ANR) y de formación (ERASMUS+).
